Codehead(hikes)

title: Univariate Viz — Exercises
text:
Exercise 2: Load tidyverse
We’ll address the above questions using ggplot tools. Try running the following chunk and simply take note of the error message – this is one you’ll get a lot!

Code# Use the ggplot function
ggplot(hikes, aes(x = rating))







In order to use ggplot tools, we have to first load the tidyverse package in which they live. We’ve installed the package but we need to tell R when we want to use it. Run the chunk below to load the library. You’ll need to do this within any .qmd file that uses ggplot().

Code# Load the package
library(tidyverse)

section: Exercise 3: Bar Chart of Ratings - Part 1
text:
Exercise 3: Bar Chart of Ratings - Part 1
Consider some specific research questions about the difficulty rating of the hikes:

How many hikes fall into each category? -There are 27 moderate hikes -There are 11 easy hikes -There are 8 hard hikes
Are the hikes evenly distributed among these categories, or are some more common than others? >Some ratings are more common than the rest of the ratings.

All of these questions can be answered with: (1) a bar chart; of (2) the categorical data recorded in the rating column. First, set up the plotting frame:

Codeggplot(hikes, aes(x = rating))







Think about:

What did this do? What do you observe? >It sets up the graph but doesn’t display data.
What, in general, is the first argument of the ggplot() function? hikes, the data
What is the purpose of writing x = rating? >It is defining the x-variable as rating.
What do you think aes stands for?!? >Aesthetic

title: Univariate Viz — Exercises
text:
Exercise 5: Bar Chart Follow-up
Part a
Reflect on the ggplot() code.

What’s the purpose of the +? When do we use it? >It adds to the existing command with additional instructions.
We added the bars using geom_bar()? Why “geom”? >Geometric
What does labs() stand for? Labels
What’s the difference between color and fill? >Color is the outline and fill is the center of the bar.
Part b
In general, bar charts allow us to examine the following properties of a categorical variable:


observed categories: What categories did we observe?

Ratings

variability between categories: Are observations evenly spread out among the categories, or are some categories more common than others? >Some categories are more common.
We must then translate this information into the context of our analysis, here hikes in the Adirondacks. Summarize below what you learned from the bar chart, in context. >There are more easy hikes in Adirondacks than any other rating of hike. The hikes tend to be easier.
Part c
Is there anything you don’t like about this barplot? For example: check out the x-axis again. >It is not in order of easy to hard.

title: Univariate Viz — Exercises
text:
Exercise 6: Sad Bar Chart
Let’s now consider some research questions related to the quantitative elevation variable:

Among the hikes, what’s the range of elevation and how are the hikes distributed within this range (eg, evenly, in clumps, “normally”)? >There are more hikes with less elevation.
What’s a typical elevation? >The most common elevation is between 4,000 to 4,200.
Are there any outliers, ie, hikes that have unusually high or low elevations? >Yes, Mt. Marcy has an elevation of 5344.

Here:

Construct a bar chart of the quantitative elevation variable.
Explain why this might not be an effective visualization for this and other quantitative variables. (What questions does / doesn’t it help answer?)


Code# write your code here
ggplot(hikes, aes(x=elevation))+ 
  geom_bar(fill = "pink")+
  labs(x="Elevation", y="Hikes")+
  theme_classic()








This graph has too many variables to effectively represent this data. It can answer the minimum and maximum elevations but does not show where the majority of data is.

title: Univariate Viz — Exercises
text:
Exercise 7: A Histogram of Elevation
Quantitative variables require different viz than categorical variables. Especially when there are many possible outcomes of the quantitative variable. It’s typically insufficient to simply count up the number of times we’ve observed a particular outcome as the bar graph did above. It gives us a sense of ranges and typical outcomes, but not a good sense of how the observations are distributed across this range. We’ll explore two methods for graphing quantitative variables: histograms and density plots.
Histograms are constructed by (1) dividing up the observed range of the variable into ‘bins’ of equal width; and (2) counting up the number of cases that fall into each bin. Check out the example below:

Part a
Let’s dig into some details.

How many hikes have an elevation between 4500 and 4700 feet? >6 hikes
How many total hikes have an elevation of at least 5100 feet? >2 hikes
Part b
Now the bigger picture. In general, histograms allow us to examine the following properties of a quantitative variable:

typical outcome: Where’s the center of the data points? What’s typical? >The center of the data and typical data is at around 4000 ft.
variability & range: How spread out are the outcomes? What are the max and min outcomes? >The max elevation is about 5500 ft and the minimum is about 3800 ft.
shape: How are values distributed along the observed range? Is the distribution symmetric, right-skewed, left-skewed, bi-modal, or uniform (flat)? >The data is skewed to the left.
outliers: Are there any outliers, ie, outcomes that are unusually large/small? T>here are no obvious outliers.

We must then translate this information into the context of our analysis, here hikes in the Adirondacks. Addressing each of the features in the above list, summarize below what you learned from the histogram, in context. >The elevation in Adirondacks is varies from 3800 ft to 5000 ft. Most of the data is around 4000 ft. There are no obvious outliers within this data set.

title: Univariate Viz — Exercises
text:
Exercise 8: Building Histograms - Part 1
2-MINUTE CHALLENGE: Thinking of the bar chart code, try to intuit what line you can tack on to the below frame of elevation to add a histogram layer. Don’t forget a +. If it doesn’t come to you within 2 minutes, no problem – all will be revealed in the next exercise.

Codeggplot(hikes, aes(x = elevation))+
  geom_histogram(fill = "navy", color = "black")+
  theme_classic()

title: Univariate Viz — Exercises
text:
Exercise 9: Building Histograms - Part 2
Let’s build some histograms. Try each chunk below, one by one. In each chunk, make a comment about how both the code and the corresponding plot both changed.

Code# This added the bars to the histogram.
ggplot(hikes, aes(x = elevation)) +
  geom_histogram()








Code# This made the outline of the bars white.
ggplot(hikes, aes(x = elevation)) +
  geom_histogram(color = "white") 








Code# This filled the bars with blue.
ggplot(hikes, aes(x = elevation)) +
  geom_histogram(color = "white", fill = "blue") 








Code# This changed the name of the axis.
ggplot(hikes, aes(x = elevation)) +
  geom_histogram(color = "white") +
  labs(x = "Elevation (feet)", y = "Number of hikes")








Code# This changed the size of the bin width.
ggplot(hikes, aes(x = elevation)) +
  geom_histogram(color = "white", binwidth = 1000) +
  labs(x = "Elevation (feet)", y = "Number of hikes")








Code# This made the bin width much smaller.
ggplot(hikes, aes(x = elevation)) +
  geom_histogram(color = "white", binwidth = 5) +
  labs(x = "Elevation (feet)", y = "Number of hikes")








Code# This bin width size is between the past two.
ggplot(hikes, aes(x = elevation)) +
  geom_histogram(color = "white", binwidth = 200) +
  labs(x = "Elevation (feet)", y = "Number of hikes")

title: Univariate Viz — Exercises
text:
Exercise 10: Histogram Follow-up

What function added the histogram layer / geometry? >geom_histogram()
What’s the difference between color and fill? Color creates an outline and fill makes the whole bar a different color.
Why does adding color = "white" improve the visualization? >It distinguishes the bars.
What did binwidth do? >It changes the size of the bar categories.
Why does the histogram become ineffective if the binwidth is too big (eg, 1000 feet)? >If the bin width is to big we cannot see how the data is distributed.
Why does the histogram become ineffective if the binwidth is too small (eg, 5 feet)? >If the bin width is too small it is hard to see what each catagory is.

title: Univariate Viz — Exercises
text:
Exercise 11: Density Plots
Density plots are essentially smooth versions of the histogram. Instead of sorting observations into discrete bins, the “density” of observations is calculated across the entire range of outcomes. The greater the number of observations, the greater the density! The density is then scaled so that the area under the density curve always equals 1 and the area under any fraction of the curve represents the fraction of cases that lie in that range.
Check out a density plot of elevation. Notice that the y-axis (density) has no contextual interpretation – it’s a relative measure. The higher the density, the more common are elevations in that range.

Codeggplot(hikes, aes(x = elevation)) +
  geom_density()







Questions


INTUITION CHECK: Before tweaking the code and thinking back to geom_bar() and geom_histogram(), how do you anticipate the following code will change the plot?

geom_density(color = "blue")
geom_density(fill = "orange")




I would guess that color changes the color of the line and fill colors the area under the graph.


TRY IT! Test out those lines in the chunk below. Was your intuition correct?


Codeggplot(hikes, aes(x = elevation)) +
  geom_density(fill="salmon", color="brown4")








Examine the density plot. How does it compare to the histogram? What does it tell you about the typical elevation, variability / range in elevations, and shape of the distribution of elevations within this range? >It is similar to the histogram but it is continuous. It shows that the typical elevation is around 4100. It shows that the range of elevation is from about 3800 to 5500 ft and that most of the elevation is in the bottom of this range.

title: Univariate Viz — Exercises
text:
Exercise 12: Density Plots vs Histograms
The histogram and density plot both allow us to visualize the behavior of a quantitative variable: typical outcome, variability / range, shape, and outliers. What are the pros/cons of each? What do you like/not like about each? > Histogram shows clear and distinct catagories. The denisty plot shows more specific data.

title: Univariate Viz — Exercises
text:
Exercise 13: Code = communication
We obviously won’t be done until we talk about communication. All code above has a similar general structure (where the details can change):

Though not necessary to the code working, it’s common, good practice to indent or tab the lines of code after the first line (counterexample below). Why?


Code# YUCK
ggplot(hikes, aes(x = elevation)) +
geom_histogram(color = "white", binwidth = 200) +
labs(x = "Elevation (feet)", y = "Number of hikes")








Though not necessary to the code working, it’s common, good practice to put a line break after each + (counterexample below). Why?


Code# YUCK 
ggplot(hikes, aes(x = elevation)) + geom_histogram(color = "white", binwidth = 200) + labs(x = "Elevation (feet)", y = "Number of hikes")

title: Bivariate Viz — Exercises
text:
Exercise 4: Visualizing Trend
The trend of the relationship between repub_pct_20 and repub_pct_16 is clearly positive and (mostly) linear. We can highlight this trend by adding a model “smooth” to the plot:

Codeggplot(elections, aes(y = repub_pct_20, x = repub_pct_16)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth()







Part a
Construct a new plot that contains the model smooth but does not include the individual point glyphs.

Codeggplot(elections, aes(x=repub_pct_16, y=repub_pct_20))+
  geom_smooth()







Part b
By default, geom_smooth() adds a smooth, localized model line. To examine the “best” linear model, we can specify method = "lm". It’s pretty similar in this example.

Codeggplot(elections, aes(y = repub_pct_20, x = repub_pct_16)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm")

Exercise 7: Quantitative vs Categorical: Violins & Boxes
Though the above scatterplot did group the counties by historical category, it’s nearly impossible to pick out meaningful patterns in 2020 Republican support in each category. Let’s try adding 2 different geom layers to the frame:

Code# Side-by-side violin plots
ggplot(elections, aes(y = repub_pct_20, x = historical)) +
  geom_violin()








Code# Side-by-side boxplots (defined below)
ggplot(elections, aes(y = repub_pct_20, x = historical)) +
  geom_boxplot()







Box plots are constructed from five numbers: the minimum, 25th percentile, median, 75th percentile, and maximum value of a quantitative variable:

section: Exercise 9: Quantitative vs Categorical: Density Plots
text:
Exercise 9: Quantitative vs Categorical: Density Plots
Work through the chunks below and address the comments therein.

Code# Name two "bad" things about this plot
# The colors do not match. You can not see all of the graphs.
ggplot(elections, aes(x = repub_pct_20, fill = historical)) +
  geom_density()








Code# What does scale_fill_manual do?
# Fills in the different denisty plots.
ggplot(elections, aes(x = repub_pct_20, fill = historical)) +
  geom_density() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("blue", "purple", "red"))








Code# What does alpha = 0.5 do? Makes the opacity of the fill different.
# Play around with different values of alpha, between 0 and 1
ggplot(elections, aes(x = repub_pct_20, fill = historical)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.4) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("blue", "purple", "red"))








Code# What does facet_wrap do?!
#Splits the graph into three smaller graphs.
ggplot(elections, aes(x = repub_pct_20, fill = historical)) +
  geom_density() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("blue", "purple", "red")) +
  facet_wrap(~historical)








Code# Let's try a similar grouping strategy with a histogram instead of density plot.
# Why is this terrible?
# Its hard to tell the difference in sizes between the three catagories.
ggplot(elections, aes(x = repub_pct_20, fill = historical)) +
  geom_histogram(color = "white") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("blue", "purple", "red"))

title: Bivariate Viz — Exercises
text:
Exercise 10: Reflect
We’ve now learned 3 (of many) ways to visualize the relationship between a quantitative and categorical variable: side-by-side violins, boxplots, and density plots.

Which do you like best? The boxplots!
What is one pro of density plots relative to boxplots? They shows more of the data.
What is one con of density plots relative to boxplots? It is harder to tell the median and other important numbers.

Exercise 11: Categorical vs Categorical: Intuition Check
Finally, let’s simply explore who won each county in 2020 (winner_20) and how this breaks down by historical voting trends in the state. That is, let’s explore the relationship between 2 categorical variables. Spend at most 5 minutes on the following intuition check. Adjust the code below to recreate the following two plots.

title: Bivariate Viz — Exercises
text:
Exercise 12: Categorical vs Categorical
Construct the following 4 bar plot visualizations.

Code# A stacked bar plot
# How are the "historical" and "winner_20" variables mapped to the plot, i.e. what roles do they play?
# Historical is on the x-axis and the winner is the stacked variable.
ggplot(elections, aes(x = historical, fill = winner_20)) +
  geom_bar()








Code# A faceted bar plot
ggplot(elections, aes(x = winner_20)) +
  geom_bar() +
  facet_wrap(~historical)








Code# A side-by-side bar plot
# Note the new argument to geom_bar
ggplot(elections, aes(x = historical, fill = winner_20)) +
  geom_bar(position = "dodge")








Code# A proportional bar plot
# Note the new argument to geom_bar
ggplot(elections, aes(x = historical, fill = winner_20)) +
  geom_bar(position = "fill")







Part a
Name one pro and one con of using the “proportional bar plot” instead of one of the other three options. A pro is that it uses the whole graph and shows percentages. A con is that the you will not get accurate counts.
Part b
What’s your favorite bar plot from part and why? The overlapping denisty plot because it shows a very clear comparison.

Import some daily weather data from a few locations in Australia:

title: Bivariate Viz — Exercises
text:
Exercise 14: State Support (Optional)
The above visualizations are foundational and important. But they’re not the only way to visualize the variables in our dataset.
Suppose we wanted to better understand how the 2020 Republican support varied from county to county within each state. Since repub_pct_20 is quantitative and state_abbr is categorical, we could make a density plot of repub_pct_20 for each state. Reflect on why this is bad.

Codeggplot(elections, aes(x = repub_pct_20, fill = state_abbr)) + 
  geom_density(alpha = 0.5)






Code# Too many states


A facet wrap would also be bad!

Codeggplot(elections, aes(x = repub_pct_20)) + 
  geom_density(alpha = 0.5) + 
  facet_wrap(~ state_abbr)






Code#Too many states.


When we want to compare the distribution of some quantitative outcome among many groups / categories, a ridgeline plot can be a good option. These are also called joy plots, named after the album cover for “Unknown Pleasures” by Joy Division. (Look it up!) To make a ridgeline plot, we can use the geom_density_ridges() function from the ggridges package.

Code# Remember to install ggridges package before calling it
library(ggridges)

# Make our first joy plot
# THINK: What DON'T you like about this?
ggplot(elections, aes(x = repub_pct_20, y = state_abbr)) + 
  geom_density_ridges()








Code# Let's put the states in order by Republican support, not alphabet
# How do you think fct_reorder works? We'll learn about this later in the semester.
ggplot(elections, aes(x = repub_pct_20, y = fct_reorder(state_abbr, repub_pct_20))) + 
  geom_density_ridges(alpha = 0.5)








Code# YOUR TURN: color/fill the ridges according to a state's historical voting patterns 
# and add meaningful axis labels
ggplot(elections, aes(x = repub_pct_20, y = fct_reorder(state_abbr, repub_pct_20), fill =  historical))+
  geom_density_ridges(alpha=0.5)+
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("blue", "purple", "red"))







Follow-up questions

Which states tend to have the most variability in outcomes from county to county? The least? Missori has a lot of variability while Hawaii has very little variability.
What other interesting patterns do you notice? Purple states have a larger spread of variation.
Does this plot prompt any other questions? Why are some red states so low in republican support and vice versa.
